issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one. 'Being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/self-directed trauma context that is not supported anywhere else in the profile and is hard to reconcile with bereavement/trauma-to-loved-one as the index trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items do not form a coherent theme. 'Talking about the future' could fit grief-related loss, but 'incomprehensible chatter' and especially 'being looked at sexually' point toward very different trauma contexts, making the trigger profile internally inconsistent for a single index trauma.

vignette: John, a 63-year-old African American journalist, has been haunted by memories of his daughter’s accident ever since it happened. He and his wife, Susan, had attended a local community event where their daughter was performing as part of her high school drama club. The night was bustling with laughter and excitement until the moment when John heard a loud crash followed by incomprehensible chatter from the audience. His initial reaction was confusion, but this quickly turned to horror as he realized that the accident involved his daughter. In the aftermath of the event, John found himself struggling to make sense of what had happened. When trying to recount the sequence of events to Susan and other family members, he often lost the thread and couldn't finish his sentences. The inability to explain clearly frustrated him deeply, as journalism has always been about conveying facts and stories in a clear and coherent manner. Since that fateful night, John's mind is constantly drawn back to the event whenever he encounters certain triggers. Talking about the future with Susan now often provokes vivid memories of that evening. When he hears incomprehensible chatter at work or social gatherings, it instantly brings him back to that moment when everything seemed chaotic and unclear. Conversations about people losing loved ones in any context also trigger intense recollections. The memory itself is particularly distressing. John can taste the same bitter flavor from that night whenever these memories return. He knows exactly what happened but often feels at a loss for words, unable to find the right way to describe it. The vividness of the taste and the intensity of his inability to articulate his experience have made it difficult for him to engage in normal daily activities. Over time, John has noticed that these triggers increasingly interfere with both his work as a journalist and his home life. He often finds himself avoiding social gatherings or professional events where such conversations might arise, fearing the intrusive memories. This avoidance has strained his relationship with Susan, who is concerned about how much he isolates himself from their shared activities. What frightens John most is not just the intensity of these memories but also the uncertainty and chaos they evoke. He had come to believe that if he could only articulate what happened more clearly, he might feel less haunted by it. However, each attempt to do so leaves him feeling lost in a sea of confusion and frustration. The tipping point came when John’s editor pointed out his declining performance at work due to frequent absences and difficulty focusing on assignments that required detailed recollections or future-oriented planning. Realizing the impact this was having on both his career and family life, he finally sought help. John is most hopeful for a way to manage these triggers and memories so that they no longer disrupt his daily functioning. He wants to regain control over his thoughts and emotions, hoping to find clarity in recounting what happened without being overwhelmed by the vividness of his experiences.
